questions.stem: The mechanical advantage of a machine is defined as the ratio of

options.text: distance moved by the effort to distance moved by the load
useful work output to total work input

questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage measures how many times the machine multiplies the force you apply, so the load you overcome goes on top and the effort you supply goes underneath. It is a ratio of two forces and therefore has no unit.

distractorRationale.a: Inverted — this would give a value less than 1 for a force-multiplying machine
distractorRationale.c: This is the definition of velocity ratio, not mechanical advantage
distractorRationale.d: This is the definition of efficiency

questions.stem: A block and tackle system has five rope sections supporting the movable block. Its velocity ratio is
questions.explanation: In a block and tackle, the effort must be pulled through a distance equal to the number of supporting rope sections multiplied by the rise of the load. With five supporting sections, the effort moves five times as far as the load, so the velocity ratio is 5.

distractorRationale.a: A velocity ratio of 1 belongs to a single fixed pulley, which only changes direction
distractorRationale.b: A velocity ratio of 2 belongs to a single movable pulley
distractorRationale.d: Doubled the number of sections, which would need ten supporting ropes

questions.stem: The efficiency of a machine is correctly given by
questions.explanation: Efficiency is useful work out over work in, which expands to $\frac{L \times d_L}{E \times d_E} = \frac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}}$. Because efficiency cannot exceed 100 %, this also tells you that MA is always smaller than VR in a real machine.

distractorRationale.a: Multiplying gives values far above 100 %, which is physically impossible
distractorRationale.b: Inverted, so it would always exceed 100 % for a real machine
distractorRationale.d: Adding two dimensionless ratios has no physical meaning and would not be a percentage

questions.stem: An effort of 200 N is used to raise a load of 600 N with a machine. Calculate the mechanical advantage of the machine.
questions.explanation: $\text{MA} = \frac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}} = \frac{600}{200} = 3$. The machine multiplies the applied force three times. Mechanical advantage has no unit because it is the ratio of two forces.

questions.stem: A plank 5.0 m long is used as an inclined plane to raise a drum onto a platform 1.0 m high. Calculate the velocity ratio of the inclined plane.
questions.explanation: For an inclined plane, $\text{VR} = \frac{\text{length of plane}}{\text{vertical height}} = \frac{5.0}{1.0} = 5$. The load is pushed 5.0 m along the slope while it rises only 1.0 m, so the effort moves five times as far as the load.

questions.stem: A block and tackle with 4 pulleys raises a load of 500 N when an effort of 150 N is applied. Calculate the efficiency of the system. Give your answer as a percentage, correct to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: $\text{MA} = \frac{500}{150} = 3.33$ and $\text{VR} = 4$ for four supporting rope sections. Efficiency $= \frac{3.33}{4} \times 100 = 83.3\%$. The missing 16.7 % goes into friction at the axles and into lifting the movable block itself.

questions.stem: A machine has a velocity ratio of 5 and an efficiency of 80 %. Its mechanical advantage is
questions.explanation: Rearranging $\eta = \frac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} \times 100$ gives $\text{MA} = \frac{\eta \times \text{VR}}{100} = \frac{80 \times 5}{100} = 4$. As expected for a real machine, MA (4) is less than VR (5).

distractorRationale.a: Divided the velocity ratio by 2.5 or misapplied the percentage
distractorRationale.c: Divided VR by the efficiency (5 ÷ 0.8), giving an MA larger than VR, which would mean over 100 % efficiency

questions.stem: For a real machine, the mechanical advantage can be greater than the velocity ratio.
questions.explanation: False. Since efficiency equals MA ÷ VR × 100 % and efficiency can never exceed 100 %, MA must always be smaller than VR. If MA exceeded VR, the machine would be delivering more energy than it received, which conservation of energy forbids.

questions.stem: A screw jack has a pitch of 0.50 cm and its handle is 35 cm long. Taking π = 22/7, calculate the velocity ratio of the jack.
questions.explanation: For a screw jack, $\text{VR} = \frac{2\pi r}{\text{pitch}}$. The handle sweeps a circle of circumference $2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 35 = 220\ \text{cm}$ per turn, while the load rises only 0.50 cm. So $\text{VR} = \frac{220}{0.50} = 440$. Such a huge velocity ratio is why one hand can raise a lorry.

questions.stem: A ramp 10 m long is used to slide a 500 N drum onto a lorry platform 2.0 m high, using an effort of 125 N along the ramp. Calculate the efficiency of the ramp. Give your answer as a percentage.
questions.explanation: $\text{VR} = \frac{10}{2.0} = 5$ and $\text{MA} = \frac{500}{125} = 4$, so efficiency $= \frac{4}{5} \times 100 = 80\%$. Checking through energies: the effort does $125 \times 10 = 1250\ \text{J}$ while the drum gains $500 \times 2.0 = 1000\ \text{J}$, and $\frac{1000}{1250} \times 100 = 80\%$.
